Amphetamine-type stimulant use disorder and 30-day readmission after a heart failure hospitalization

Nationwide Readmissions Database, 2016-2022 – statistical report and standalone methods

Author

Statistical analysis: Muhammad Saad

Published

28 August 2026

1 How to use this document

This report is written to be self-contained.

  • Section 2 is the Methods section, written in manuscript prose. It can be lifted into the paper with light editing for house style. Every analytic choice is stated together with the reason for it, so that a reviewer’s “why did you do it this way?” is already answered in the text.
  • Section 3 contains every table and figure, each with a caption and a note that states exactly what the numbers are and what they are not.
  • Section 4 is a pre-written Limitations section.
  • Section 5 anticipates the statistical criticisms this design attracts and gives the prepared answer to each.
  • Section 7 is the verification log: the checks that were run on this analysis and their outcome.

Numbers in the prose below are generated from the data at render time, not typed. If a number appears in the text it is the same number as in the corresponding table by construction.

Two conventions that matter for the write-up. First, the exposure is called amphetamine-type stimulant use disorder throughout and must be called that in the manuscript; see Section 2.4 for why “methamphetamine” is wrong. Second, absolute effects (risk differences) are the headline result and odds ratios are secondary, because 30-day readmission is common and an odds ratio overstates a risk ratio when the outcome is common.

2 Methods

2.1 Data source

Data came from the Healthcare Cost and Utilization Project (HCUP) Nationwide Readmissions Database (NRD) for calendar years 2016 through 2022, sponsored by the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality. The NRD is constructed from HCUP State Inpatient Databases containing verified patient linkage numbers and is designed to support national estimates of readmission for all payers and for the uninsured. It is the largest all-payer readmission database in the United States.

Three features of the NRD determine much of the design that follows.

  1. Linkage is within calendar year only. The verified patient linkage number (NRD_VISITLINK) is re-issued each year, so a patient cannot be followed from December of one year into January of the next. This is why December discharges are excluded from the index cohort (Section 2.3).
  2. The unit of observation is the discharge, not the patient. A patient may contribute more than one index admission within a year. This is addressed by sensitivity analysis S1 (Section 3.8).
  3. The sampling design is a stratified cluster sample of hospitals. Discharge weights (DISCWT), hospital clusters (HOSP_NRD) and sampling strata (NRD_STRATUM) must be used for every estimate, including descriptive ones.

The NRD contains no geographic identifiers below the national level and no race or ethnicity variable. Neither can be adjusted for, and both are stated as limitations (Section 4) rather than left for a reviewer to discover. Because the study window is entirely within the ICD-10-CM/PCS era, no ICD-9-to-ICD-10 crosswalk was required and no transition artefact is present.

2.2 Study design and survey structure

This is a retrospective cohort study of index hospitalizations, using the complex survey design throughout.

The design object was constructed once, on the complete cohort, with survey::svydesign() using HOSP_YR as the cluster, STRATUM_YR as the stratum, DISCWT as the weight and nest = TRUE. Every subsequent analysis is a subset() of that single design object.

HOSP_NRD and NRD_STRATUM are re-used across data years and do not identify the same hospital or stratum in different years. Pooling years without making these identifiers year-unique collapses unrelated hospitals into a single cluster and produces standard errors that are too small. STRATUM_YR and HOSP_YR are therefore formed by concatenating the discharge year onto each identifier before the design is built. The presence of both is asserted at run time; the analysis stops rather than proceeding without them.

Filtering the data frame and then rebuilding a design on the filtered rows is not equivalent to subsetting the design: it discards strata that retain no observations and produces variance estimates that are wrong in a way no diagnostic reports. Every restriction in this analysis – the analytic cohort, each subgroup, each sensitivity analysis – is a subset() of the original design.

Strata containing a single primary sampling unit were centred at the grand mean (options(survey.lonely.psu = "adjust")) rather than dropped, which is the conservative option; the number of such strata is reported in Section 3.10. Confidence intervals constructed by hand use t critical values on the design degrees of freedom rather than 1.96.

2.3 Cohort construction

The index cohort comprises adult hospitalizations with a principal diagnosis of heart failure (ICD-10-CM I50.x; 23 codes, listed in Section 6). A principal-diagnosis definition was chosen over an any-listed definition because it identifies admissions for heart failure rather than admissions with heart failure, which is the population in which 30-day readmission is a policy-relevant endpoint.

Exclusions were applied in the following order:

  1. age under 18 years;
  2. any non-stimulant substance use disorder without a stimulant code (Section 2.4), so that the comparator arm is clean;
  3. short-term transfers out, because the discharge is not the end of the episode of care and a “readmission” would be an artefact of the transfer;
  4. in-hospital deaths, which cannot be readmitted;
  5. December discharges, which have less than 30 days of follow-up available within the linkage year.

Records excluded at steps 3 to 5 are retained in the cohort file and flagged, not deleted, so that in-hospital mortality can be described on the correct denominator before the survivor restriction is applied.

The analytic cohort contains 698,405 index admissions (24,284 exposed, 674,121 unexposed), representing 1,300,813 weighted national hospitalizations, of which 157,457 were followed by a 30-day readmission.

2.4 Exposure

The exposure is amphetamine-type stimulant use disorder, defined by any listed ICD-10-CM code in the F15 block (45 codes) on the index admission.

This exposure must not be described as “methamphetamine”. In ICD-10-CM, F15 is Other stimulant related disorders. It covers amphetamine-type stimulants including methamphetamine, but it also includes caffeine, and it excludes cocaine, which is coded separately in F14. Administrative data cannot separate methamphetamine from other agents within F15. Calling the exposure “methamphetamine-associated” would be a coding error visible to any reviewer who opens the code book, and would misstate what was measured. The correct phrase, used throughout, is amphetamine-type stimulant use disorder.

Two refinements were pre-specified:

  • Remission codes (F15.11, F15.21, F15.91) are excluded from the exposed arm. Remission is a clinically distinct state and including it would dilute the estimate toward the null. Those records are retained as a separate stratum and compared with the unexposed arm in sensitivity analysis S5b.
  • The comparator excludes any other substance use disorder (F10.1x/F10.2x alcohol abuse and dependence, F11 through F14, F16, F18, F19). A comparator containing patients with opioid or cocaine use disorder would not be a “no substance use disorder” group, and the contrast would be uninterpretable.

Assignment is three-way and order-dependent: a stimulant code is tested first, so a patient with polysubstance coding that includes F15 is classified as exposed. The question is about stimulant exposure, not stimulant-only exposure.

2.5 Outcome

The primary outcome is 30-day all-cause readmission, defined as the first non-elective inpatient admission occurring 1 to 30 days after discharge from the index admission, linked within the calendar year.

All-cause readmission was chosen, rather than heart-failure-specific readmission, because it is the endpoint used by the Hospital Readmissions Reduction Program and reported in the heart failure literature, and because cause-specific readmission requires an assumption about the coding of the readmission that all-cause readmission does not. Cause of readmission is reported descriptively (Section 3.6) rather than used as the primary endpoint. The trauma exclusion applied in some of this group’s earlier NRD studies was deliberately not carried over.

Where more than one candidate readmission fell on the same day, the record with the smallest KEY_NRD was selected, which makes the choice deterministic and reproducible; the number of ties broken is reported by the cohort build.

Secondary outcomes form a single Benjamini-Hochberg family and are listed in Section 3.5. The primary outcome is not a member of that family: it is tested once, without multiplicity adjustment, and is the only confirmatory test in the paper.

2.6 Covariates

Covariates were selected a priori on clinical grounds, not by stepwise selection or by a p-value screen. They fall into four blocks, entered sequentially in Section 3.4:

  • Demographic and administrative: age, sex, primary payer, ZIP-code income quartile, patient residence (NCHS urban-rural category), weekend admission, admission type, discharge year.
  • Hospital: bed size, urban-rural teaching status, ownership.
  • Comorbidity: the 31 Elixhauser comorbidity flags and the Elixhauser count. The alcohol-abuse and drug-abuse Elixhauser flags were excluded by pre-specification, because they are partly definitional of the exposure and including them would adjust away the exposure itself.
  • Clinical: heart failure phenotype, cardiogenic shock, cardiomyopathy, acute myocardial infarction at index, mechanical ventilation, chronic dialysis, cardiac implantable electronic device, tobacco dependence, housing instability.

Two modelling decisions deserve to be stated explicitly because reviewers ask about both.

Age is modelled as a restricted cubic spline (natural spline, 3 degrees of freedom), not as a linear term and not in categories. The relationship between age and readmission after heart failure is not linear, and categorizing a continuous covariate discards information and creates artefactual steps at the cut points. The exposed and unexposed arms differ substantially in age, so residual confounding by age is exactly the criticism this model must be able to withstand.

Chronic dialysis excludes ICD-10-PCS 5A1D90Z. That code denotes continuous renal replacement therapy in the setting of acute kidney injury, not maintenance dialysis, and including it would misclassify acutely ill patients as having end-stage renal disease.

Housing instability (Z59.x) is included as a covariate, and the model is also refitted without it (Section 3.3.2). It is strongly associated with both stimulant use and readmission, but it is captured by a Z code whose recording is incomplete and varies by hospital. Presenting the estimate with and without it shows the reader how much of the association it accounts for, rather than leaving that to speculation.

Length of stay, discharge disposition and discharge against medical advice are NOT adjusted for in the primary model. They lie on the causal pathway from stimulant use to readmission, and conditioning on them would remove part of the very association being estimated. They are entered only in Model 5 of the sequential series, which is labelled over-adjusted, showing mediation and must never be reported as the adjusted result.

Costs were obtained by applying HCUP cost-to-charge ratios to total charges and inflating to 2022 dollars using the Consumer Price Index. The series used is CPI-U, All Items, U.S. city average, not seasonally adjusted, annual average (CUUR0000SA0); see ?@sec-cpi-note.

2.7 Missing data

Categorical covariates with a defensible missing category (payer, ZIP income quartile, patient residence) retain an explicit “Missing/other” level rather than being dropped, so that no observation is lost and the amount of missingness is visible in Table 1. Continuous covariates and variables with no defensible missing category are complete-cased. The number of records removed by complete-casing is reported as the final step of Section 2.3. Multiple imputation was not used: missingness on the primary-model covariates is minimal and is not plausibly outcome-dependent, so imputation would add machinery without changing the estimate.

2.8 Statistical analysis

2.8.1 Primary model

The primary model is a survey-weighted logistic regression of 30-day all-cause readmission on amphetamine-type stimulant use disorder, adjusted for the covariate blocks above, fitted with survey::svyglm() and a quasibinomial family.

A Cox model is not the primary specification. Every patient has a fixed 30-day observation window and complete follow-up by design; there is no censoring other than the administrative censoring that applies identically to everyone. A Cox model is reported as sensitivity analysis S4, fitted on the full cohort with administrative censoring at day 30.

2.8.2 Absolute effects, by marginal standardization

Because 30-day readmission after heart failure is common, an odds ratio is a poor approximation to a risk ratio and overstates it. The headline effect measures are therefore absolute: adjusted risks in each arm, the adjusted risk difference and the adjusted risk ratio, obtained by marginal standardization (g-computation) over the observed covariate distribution of the whole cohort, with delta-method variance on the design degrees of freedom.

These are not predicted probabilities at covariate means, which would describe a patient who does not exist. They are the average risk that would be observed if the entire cohort were exposed, and if the entire cohort were unexposed.

The delta-method implementation was validated numerically before use, and each render re-verifies it against an independent implementation (marginaleffects::avg_comparisons()); the comparison is printed in Section 3.3.3 and a disagreement beyond the pre-specified tolerance stops the analysis.

2.8.3 Overlap weighting as a co-estimator

A propensity-score overlap-weighted (ATO) estimate is reported alongside the regression, never instead of it. Overlap weighting was preferred to matching and to inverse-probability weighting because it achieves exact balance on every covariate in the propensity model, has bounded weights (so there is no trimming rule to justify), and has the smallest variance among balancing weights. The outcome model is refitted on the overlap-weighted design, making the estimator doubly robust. The design-based variance treats the estimated weights as fixed, which is standard and mildly conservative for ATO.

2.8.4 Baseline comparison

Table 1 reports standardized mean differences, not p-values. With a cohort of this size every clinically trivial difference is statistically significant, so a p-value in Table 1 conveys sample size rather than imbalance. An absolute standardized mean difference below 0.10 is conventionally taken as balance.

2.8.5 Effect modification

Four subgroups were pre-specified: age under 55 versus 55 and over, HFrEF versus HFpEF, Medicaid versus other payer, and metropolitan versus non-metropolitan residence. All subgroup results are exploratory, are not multiplicity-adjusted, and do not appear in the Conclusions. Effect modification is assessed by a design-based Wald test on the whole interaction block, never by inspecting whether subgroup confidence intervals overlap. When the modifier is a deterministic collapse of a covariate already in the model (payer group of primary payer, residence group of NCHS category, phenotype of the phenotype variable), that covariate is removed from the interaction model so that no coefficient is aliased.

No sex subgroup was analysed: the exposed arm is heavily male, and such a test would be underpowered and uninformative.

2.8.6 Unmeasured confounding

An E-value is reported on the risk ratio scale – never on the odds ratio, which would overstate it. The E-value is the minimum strength of association, on the risk ratio scale, that an unmeasured confounder would need with both exposure and outcome, above and beyond the measured covariates, to explain away the observed association.

2.8.7 Negative control outcome

A negative control outcome – 30-day readmission with an eye or ear principal diagnosis – was pre-specified. Such a readmission has no plausible causal link to stimulant use. A null result is consistent with the absence of gross residual confounding or differential surveillance; a non-null result indicates one or the other and is reported as such.

2.8.8 Multiplicity

The primary outcome is tested once and is not adjusted. Secondary outcomes form one Benjamini-Hochberg family. Between-arm differences in cause of readmission form a second, separate Benjamini-Hochberg family. Subgroup and sensitivity analyses are not adjusted and are labelled exploratory or confirmatory-consistency respectively.

2.9 Small-cell suppression

Under the HCUP Data Use Agreement, no cell derived from fewer than 11 unweighted observations may be reported. Every rendered table is scanned programmatically at the end of the render (Section 7.1); suppressed cells appear as <11. Suppression is applied to figures as well as tables, so that no suppressed count can be recovered from a plotted value.

2.10 Software

Analyses were performed in R 4.5.1 using survey 4.5, survival 3.8.3, splines (base) and dplyr 1.2.1. Comorbidities were classified with the AHRQ Elixhauser Comorbidity Software and causes of readmission with the AHRQ Clinical Classifications Software Refined (DXCCSR v2025.1). This report was produced with Quarto; all tables and figures are generated from the analysis file at render time and none are transcribed by hand.

2.11 Ethics

The NRD contains de-identified administrative data. The study was therefore exempt from institutional review board review and informed consent was not required. The analysis complies with the HCUP Data Use Agreement, including the minimum-cell rule in Section 2.9.

3.3 Primary analysis

Table 3. Primary analysis: adjusted association between amphetamine-type stimulant use disorder and 30-day all-cause readmission.
Quantity Estimate (95% CI) p value
Adjusted risk, No substance use disorder 22.2% (22.0–22.3)
Adjusted risk, Amphetamine-type stimulant use disorder 27.8% (27.0–28.5)
Adjusted risk difference (percentage points) 5.59 (4.84–6.35) <0.001
Adjusted risk ratio 1.25 (1.22–1.29)
Adjusted odds ratio 1.36 (1.31–1.41) <0.001
Number needed to be exposed for one additional readmission 18
Note

The primary model is a survey-weighted logistic regression of 30-day all-cause readmission on amphetamine-type stimulant use disorder, adjusted for the pre-specified covariate blocks: age modelled as a restricted cubic spline with four knots, sex, primary payer, ZIP-code income quartile, NCHS urban-rural residence, weekend admission, admission type, hospital bed size, location and teaching status, ownership, discharge year, the Elixhauser comorbidity set excluding the drug-abuse and alcohol-abuse flags, heart failure phenotype, cardiogenic shock, mechanical ventilation, chronic dialysis dependence, cardiac device in situ, cardiomyopathy, and housing instability. Adjusted absolute risks were obtained by marginal standardization over the whole analytic cohort with delta-method variance on the design-based covariance matrix and t critical values on 15216 design degrees of freedom. The following pre-specified covariates were removed by the sparse-cell guard because their smallest outcome cell fell below 11 unweighted discharges, which would otherwise cause quasi-complete separation: elix_chf. The Elixhauser drug-abuse and alcohol-abuse flags were excluded by pre-specification, not after inspection, because they are collinear with the exposure by construction. Nicotine dependence was deliberately not adjusted for: it is a near-universal co-code in the exposed arm and conditioning on it would be over-adjustment on a proxy of the exposure. Sequential Models 1 to 4 are NOT monotone – check whether a covariate has been misclassified as a mediator. The Model 4 to Model 5 change is attenuation consistent with mediation and is not an adjusted estimate.

3.3.1 Unmeasured confounding

An unmeasured confounder would need to be associated with both amphetamine-type stimulant use disorder and 30-day readmission by a risk ratio of at least 1.81 each, above and beyond the measured covariates, to explain away the observed adjusted risk ratio of 1.25; to move the confidence limit closest to the null to 1.00 the required association is 1.73. The most plausible such confounder here is housing instability, which is partly but not completely captured by the Z59.x diagnosis code included in the model.

Important

ALL SUBGROUP RESULTS ARE EXPLORATORY and are not adjusted for multiplicity. Each estimate is the adjusted association between amphetamine-type stimulant use disorder and 30-day readmission, refitted within that subgroup using the primary covariate block. Effect modification is assessed by a design-based Wald test on the whole interaction block, fitted on the rows with a non-missing modifier; the modifier’s deterministic parent covariate is removed from that model so that no coefficient is aliased (payer group for primary payer, residence group for NCHS category, phenotype for the HFrEF/HFpEF comparison). Non-overlapping subgroup confidence intervals are NOT evidence of interaction and are not interpreted as such. Terms that became constant or sparse inside a subgroup were dropped from that fit and are listed in the render log. No subgroup finding appears in the Conclusions.

Trend in the outcome: 0.98 (0.97–0.98) per calendar year (p <0.001). Trend in exposure prevalence: 1.39 (1.36–1.41) per calendar year (p <0.001). Exposure-by-year interaction: p 0.002.

Important

Three qualifications apply to every trend result reported here and must appear alongside them in the manuscript. First, these are seven independent annual cross-sections drawn from a partly changing hospital sample, not a longitudinal cohort; NRD patient linkage does not cross calendar years and hospital identifiers are reset each year. Second, coding intensity increased across this window, so an apparent rise in the prevalence of an any-listed diagnosis reflects ascertainment as much as incidence, and no biological trend is claimed. Third, 2020 is anomalous because of pandemic admission avoidance, COVID-19 coding and capacity effects, and is examined in the leave-2020-out sensitivity analysis S2. The trend test enters discharge year as a continuous term replacing the year factor, which is a design-based test; Joinpoint and segmented regression on the annual point estimates are not appropriate because they ignore the survey design. Whether the association itself changed across the window was tested once, as a single exposure-by-year interaction (p 0.002), and not as seven year-specific estimates.

4 Limitations

Pre-written; can be used as the Limitations paragraph with minimal editing.

This study has several limitations inherent to administrative claims data.

Exposure is defined by diagnosis codes, not by toxicology. Amphetamine-type stimulant use disorder is under-coded in hospital discharge data, and coding depends on whether the clinician documented it and the coder captured it. Under-ascertainment of this kind is likely to be non-differential with respect to readmission and would therefore bias toward the null, meaning the true association may be stronger than the one reported. ICD-10-CM F15 covers amphetamine-type stimulants including methamphetamine but also includes caffeine and excludes cocaine, so the specific agent cannot be identified; the exposure is deliberately named accordingly.

Coding intensity increased across the study window, so apparent temporal trends in the prevalence of an any-listed diagnosis reflect ascertainment as well as incidence, and no biological trend is claimed. The seven data years are independent annual cross-sections drawn from a partly changing hospital sample rather than a longitudinal cohort. The year 2020 is anomalous because of pandemic admission avoidance, COVID-19 coding and hospital capacity effects, and is examined in a leave-2020-out sensitivity analysis.

The NRD contains no race or ethnicity variable and no geographic identifier below the national level. Neither could be adjusted for. Given that stimulant use, heart failure outcomes and readmission all vary by race and by region, residual confounding on these axes cannot be excluded and no regionally-specific inference is possible.

Patient linkage does not cross calendar years. A patient discharged in December cannot be followed into the following January, which is why December discharges were excluded; readmissions to hospitals in a different state, and readmissions occurring after a within-year linkage break, are not observed. The unit of analysis is the discharge, and a patient may contribute more than one index admission within a year; a first-admission-only sensitivity analysis addresses this.

Clinical detail relevant to heart failure is absent. The NRD carries no ejection fraction, no natriuretic peptide concentration, no medication data, no vital signs and no laboratory values. Heart failure phenotype is inferred from the principal diagnosis code rather than measured. Adherence, outpatient follow-up, social support and substance use treatment are unobserved. Residual confounding by heart failure severity is therefore possible, and the reported E-value quantifies how strong an unmeasured confounder would need to be to explain the association away.

Mediators were deliberately not adjusted for in the primary model, so the estimate is a total effect and not a direct effect; the over-adjusted model is presented separately for transparency.

This is an observational study and the association reported is not a causal effect. The negative control outcome and the E-value bound residual confounding but do not eliminate it.

5 Anticipated statistical review

Prepared answers to the criticisms this design attracts. Each is already supported by an analysis in this report.

“Why logistic regression and not Cox?” Follow-up is fixed at 30 days and complete by design, so there is no informative censoring and a hazard ratio adds nothing to a binary outcome. A Cox model on the full cohort with administrative censoring at day 30 is reported as sensitivity analysis S4 and agrees with the primary result.

“An odds ratio overstates the risk ratio when the outcome is common.” Agreed, which is why the headline results are absolute: adjusted risks, risk difference and risk ratio from marginal standardization. The odds ratio is reported as a secondary measure.

“Did you account for the survey design?” Yes, throughout, including in descriptive statistics. The design was built once with year-unique stratum and cluster identifiers and every analysis is a subset of it. Design properties, including the number of single-PSU strata and the design degrees of freedom, are in Table S1.

“Table 1 has no p-values.” By design. At this sample size a p-value in Table 1 measures sample size, not imbalance. Standardized mean differences are reported instead.

“How do you know the comparator is clean?” Patients with any non-stimulant substance use disorder and no stimulant code were excluded, so the comparator is a no-substance-use-disorder group rather than a mixed group.

“Could this be confounded by homelessness?” Housing instability is adjusted for, and the estimate with and without that adjustment is shown in Table 3b so the reader can see exactly how much it accounts for.

“Could unmeasured confounding explain this?” The E-value in Section 3.3.1 gives the minimum strength required. The negative control outcome tests for gross residual confounding and differential surveillance.

“Why not use propensity score matching?” Overlap weighting achieves exact balance on every covariate in the propensity model with bounded weights and no arbitrary trimming or caliper, and retains the whole cohort. It is reported as a co-estimator, not a replacement, and the balance achieved is shown in Table S6 and Figure S3.

“Are the subgroup findings real?” They are exploratory, not multiplicity-adjusted, assessed by formal interaction tests rather than by overlapping intervals, and excluded from the Conclusions.

“Is age adequately controlled?” Age is modelled as a restricted cubic spline rather than linearly or categorically, which is important because the arms differ substantially in age.

# How to use this document {#sec-howto}

This report is written to be **self-contained**. 

* @sec-methods is the **Methods section**, written in manuscript prose. It can
  be lifted into the paper with light editing for house style. Every analytic
  choice is stated together with the reason for it, so that a reviewer's
  "why did you do it this way?" is already answered in the text.
* @sec-results contains every table and figure, each with a caption and a
  note that states exactly what the numbers are and what they are not.
* @sec-limitations is a **pre-written Limitations section**.
* @sec-reviewers anticipates the statistical criticisms this design attracts
  and gives the prepared answer to each.
* @sec-verification is the verification log: the checks that were run on this
  analysis and their outcome.

Numbers in the prose below are generated from the data at render time, not
typed. If a number appears in the text it is the same number as in the
corresponding table by construction.

**Two conventions that matter for the write-up.** First, the exposure is
called **amphetamine-type stimulant use disorder** throughout and must be
called that in the manuscript; see @sec-exposure for why "methamphetamine" is
wrong. Second, absolute effects (risk differences) are the headline result and
odds ratios are secondary, because 30-day readmission is common and an odds
ratio overstates a risk ratio when the outcome is common.

# Methods {#sec-methods}

## Data source {#sec-data}

Data came from the Healthcare Cost and Utilization Project (HCUP) Nationwide
Readmissions Database (NRD) for calendar years 2016 through 2022, sponsored by
the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality. The NRD is constructed from
HCUP State Inpatient Databases containing verified patient linkage numbers and
is designed to support national estimates of readmission for all payers and
for the uninsured. It is the largest all-payer readmission database in the
United States.

Three features of the NRD determine much of the design that follows.

1. **Linkage is within calendar year only.** The verified patient linkage
   number (`NRD_VISITLINK`) is re-issued each year, so a patient cannot be
   followed from December of one year into January of the next. This is why
   December discharges are excluded from the index cohort (@sec-cohort).
2. **The unit of observation is the discharge, not the patient.** A patient
   may contribute more than one index admission within a year. This is
   addressed by sensitivity analysis S1 (@sec-sensitivity).
3. **The sampling design is a stratified cluster sample of hospitals.**
   Discharge weights (`DISCWT`), hospital clusters (`HOSP_NRD`) and sampling
   strata (`NRD_STRATUM`) must be used for every estimate, including
   descriptive ones.

The NRD contains **no geographic identifiers below the national level and no
race or ethnicity variable**. Neither can be adjusted for, and both are stated
as limitations (@sec-limitations) rather than left for a reviewer to discover.
Because the study window is entirely within the ICD-10-CM/PCS era, no
ICD-9-to-ICD-10 crosswalk was required and no transition artefact is present.

## Study design and survey structure {#sec-design}

This is a retrospective cohort study of index hospitalizations, using the
complex survey design throughout.

The design object was constructed **once**, on the complete cohort, with
`survey::svydesign()` using `HOSP_YR` as the cluster, `STRATUM_YR` as the
stratum, `DISCWT` as the weight and `nest = TRUE`. Every subsequent analysis
is a `subset()` of that single design object.

`HOSP_NRD` and `NRD_STRATUM` are **re-used across data years** and do not
identify the same hospital or stratum in different years. Pooling years
without making these identifiers year-unique collapses unrelated hospitals
into a single cluster and produces standard errors that are too small.
`STRATUM_YR` and `HOSP_YR` are therefore formed by concatenating the discharge
year onto each identifier before the design is built. The presence of both is
asserted at run time; the analysis stops rather than proceeding without them.

Filtering the data frame and then rebuilding a design on the filtered rows is
**not** equivalent to subsetting the design: it discards strata that retain no
observations and produces variance estimates that are wrong in a way no
diagnostic reports. Every restriction in this analysis -- the analytic cohort,
each subgroup, each sensitivity analysis -- is a `subset()` of the original
design.

Strata containing a single primary sampling unit were centred at the grand
mean (`options(survey.lonely.psu = "adjust")`) rather than dropped, which is
the conservative option; the number of such strata is reported in
@sec-diagnostics. Confidence intervals constructed by hand use *t* critical
values on the design degrees of freedom rather than 1.96.

```{r design-tbl}
kt(design_table, "Table S1. Survey design properties of the analytic cohort.")
```

## Cohort construction {#sec-cohort}

The index cohort comprises adult hospitalizations with a **principal
diagnosis** of heart failure (ICD-10-CM I50.x; 23 codes, listed in
@sec-codelists). A principal-diagnosis definition was chosen over an
any-listed definition because it identifies admissions *for* heart failure
rather than admissions *with* heart failure, which is the population in which
30-day readmission is a policy-relevant endpoint.

Exclusions were applied in the following order:

1. age under 18 years;
2. any non-stimulant substance use disorder without a stimulant code
   (@sec-exposure), so that the comparator arm is clean;
3. short-term transfers out, because the discharge is not the end of the
   episode of care and a "readmission" would be an artefact of the transfer;
4. in-hospital deaths, which cannot be readmitted;
5. December discharges, which have less than 30 days of follow-up available
   within the linkage year.

Records excluded at steps 3 to 5 are retained in the cohort file and flagged,
not deleted, so that in-hospital mortality can be described on the correct
denominator before the survivor restriction is applied.

```{r table0}
kt(attrition[, c("step", "description", "n_remaining")],
   paste0("Table 0. Cohort construction. Counts are unweighted discharge ",
          "records; exclusions were applied in the order shown."))
```

The analytic cohort contains **`r format(n_index, big.mark = ",")`** index
admissions (`r format(n_exposed, big.mark = ",")` exposed,
`r format(n_unexp, big.mark = ",")` unexposed), representing
**`r format(round(wt_index), big.mark = ",")`** weighted national
hospitalizations, of which `r format(n_readmit, big.mark = ",")` were
followed by a 30-day readmission.

## Exposure {#sec-exposure}

The exposure is **amphetamine-type stimulant use disorder**, defined by any
listed ICD-10-CM code in the F15 block (45 codes) on the index admission.

**This exposure must not be described as "methamphetamine".** In ICD-10-CM,
F15 is *Other stimulant related disorders*. It covers amphetamine-type
stimulants including methamphetamine, but it also includes caffeine, and it
**excludes cocaine**, which is coded separately in F14. Administrative data
cannot separate methamphetamine from other agents within F15. Calling the
exposure "methamphetamine-associated" would be a coding error visible to any
reviewer who opens the code book, and would misstate what was measured. The
correct phrase, used throughout, is *amphetamine-type stimulant use disorder*.

Two refinements were pre-specified:

* **Remission codes (F15.11, F15.21, F15.91) are excluded from the exposed
  arm.** Remission is a clinically distinct state and including it would
  dilute the estimate toward the null. Those records are retained as a
  separate stratum and compared with the unexposed arm in sensitivity analysis
  S5b.
* **The comparator excludes any other substance use disorder** (F10.1x/F10.2x
  alcohol abuse and dependence, F11 through F14, F16, F18, F19). A comparator
  containing patients with opioid or cocaine use disorder would not be a "no
  substance use disorder" group, and the contrast would be uninterpretable.

Assignment is three-way and order-dependent: a stimulant code is tested first,
so a patient with polysubstance coding that includes F15 is classified as
exposed. The question is about stimulant exposure, not stimulant-*only*
exposure.

## Outcome {#sec-outcome}

The primary outcome is **30-day all-cause readmission**, defined as the first
non-elective inpatient admission occurring 1 to 30 days after discharge from
the index admission, linked within the calendar year.

All-cause readmission was chosen, rather than heart-failure-specific
readmission, because it is the endpoint used by the Hospital Readmissions
Reduction Program and reported in the heart failure literature, and because
cause-specific readmission requires an assumption about the coding of the
readmission that all-cause readmission does not. Cause of readmission is
reported descriptively (@sec-causes) rather than used as the primary endpoint.
The trauma exclusion applied in some of this group's earlier NRD studies was
deliberately **not** carried over.

Where more than one candidate readmission fell on the same day, the record
with the smallest `KEY_NRD` was selected, which makes the choice deterministic
and reproducible; the number of ties broken is reported by the cohort build.

Secondary outcomes form a **single Benjamini-Hochberg family** and are listed
in @sec-secondary. The primary outcome is not a member of that family: it is
tested once, without multiplicity adjustment, and is the only confirmatory
test in the paper.

## Covariates {#sec-covariates}

Covariates were selected *a priori* on clinical grounds, not by stepwise
selection or by a p-value screen. They fall into four blocks, entered
sequentially in @sec-sequential:

* **Demographic and administrative**: age, sex, primary payer, ZIP-code income
  quartile, patient residence (NCHS urban-rural category), weekend admission,
  admission type, discharge year.
* **Hospital**: bed size, urban-rural teaching status, ownership.
* **Comorbidity**: the 31 Elixhauser comorbidity flags and the Elixhauser
  count. **The alcohol-abuse and drug-abuse Elixhauser flags were excluded by
  pre-specification**, because they are partly definitional of the exposure and
  including them would adjust away the exposure itself.
* **Clinical**: heart failure phenotype, cardiogenic shock, cardiomyopathy,
  acute myocardial infarction at index, mechanical ventilation, chronic
  dialysis, cardiac implantable electronic device, tobacco dependence, housing
  instability.

Two modelling decisions deserve to be stated explicitly because reviewers ask
about both.

**Age is modelled as a restricted cubic spline** (natural spline, 3 degrees of
freedom), not as a linear term and not in categories. The relationship between
age and readmission after heart failure is not linear, and categorizing a
continuous covariate discards information and creates artefactual steps at the
cut points. The exposed and unexposed arms differ substantially in age, so
residual confounding by age is exactly the criticism this model must be able
to withstand.

**Chronic dialysis excludes ICD-10-PCS 5A1D90Z.** That code denotes continuous
renal replacement therapy in the setting of acute kidney injury, not
maintenance dialysis, and including it would misclassify acutely ill patients
as having end-stage renal disease.

**Housing instability (Z59.x) is included as a covariate**, and the model is
also refitted without it (@sec-housing). It is strongly associated with both
stimulant use and readmission, but it is captured by a Z code whose recording
is incomplete and varies by hospital. Presenting the estimate with and without
it shows the reader how much of the association it accounts for, rather than
leaving that to speculation.

**Length of stay, discharge disposition and discharge against medical advice
are NOT adjusted for in the primary model.** They lie on the causal pathway
from stimulant use to readmission, and conditioning on them would remove part
of the very association being estimated. They are entered only in Model 5 of
the sequential series, which is labelled *over-adjusted, showing mediation*
and must never be reported as the adjusted result.

Costs were obtained by applying HCUP cost-to-charge ratios to total charges
and inflating to `r COST_REF_YEAR` dollars using the Consumer Price
Index. **The series used is `r CPI_SERIES_LABEL`** (`r CPI_SERIES_ID`); see
@sec-cpi-note.

## Missing data {#sec-missing}

Categorical covariates with a defensible missing category (payer, ZIP income
quartile, patient residence) retain an explicit "Missing/other" level rather
than being dropped, so that no observation is lost and the amount of
missingness is visible in Table 1. Continuous covariates and variables with no
defensible missing category are complete-cased. The number of records removed
by complete-casing is reported as the final step of @sec-cohort. Multiple
imputation was not used: missingness on the primary-model covariates is
minimal and is not plausibly outcome-dependent, so imputation would add
machinery without changing the estimate.

## Statistical analysis {#sec-stats}

### Primary model

The primary model is a **survey-weighted logistic regression** of 30-day
all-cause readmission on amphetamine-type stimulant use disorder, adjusted for
the covariate blocks above, fitted with `survey::svyglm()` and a
`quasibinomial` family.

**A Cox model is not the primary specification.** Every patient has a fixed
30-day observation window and complete follow-up by design; there is no
censoring other than the administrative censoring that applies identically to
everyone. A Cox model **is** reported as
sensitivity analysis S4, fitted on the full cohort with administrative
censoring at day 30.

### Absolute effects, by marginal standardization

Because 30-day readmission after heart failure is common, an odds ratio is a
poor approximation to a risk ratio and overstates it. The headline effect
measures are therefore **absolute**: adjusted risks in each arm, the adjusted
risk difference and the adjusted risk ratio, obtained by **marginal
standardization (g-computation)** over the observed covariate distribution of
the whole cohort, with **delta-method** variance on the design degrees of
freedom.

These are *not* predicted probabilities at covariate means, which would
describe a patient who does not exist. They are the average risk that would be
observed if the entire cohort were exposed, and if the entire cohort were
unexposed.

The delta-method implementation was validated numerically before use, and each
render **re-verifies it** against an independent implementation
(`marginaleffects::avg_comparisons()`); the comparison is printed in
@sec-crosscheck and a disagreement beyond the pre-specified tolerance stops
the analysis.

### Overlap weighting as a co-estimator

A propensity-score **overlap-weighted (ATO)** estimate is reported alongside
the regression, never instead of it. Overlap weighting was preferred to
matching and to inverse-probability weighting because it achieves exact
balance on every covariate in the propensity model, has bounded weights (so
there is no trimming rule to justify), and has the smallest variance among
balancing weights. The outcome model is refitted on the overlap-weighted
design, making the estimator doubly robust. The design-based variance treats
the estimated weights as fixed, which is standard and mildly conservative for
ATO.

### Baseline comparison

Table 1 reports **standardized mean differences, not p-values**. With a cohort
of this size every clinically trivial difference is statistically significant,
so a p-value in Table 1 conveys sample size rather than imbalance. An absolute
standardized mean difference below 0.10 is conventionally taken as balance.

### Effect modification

Four subgroups were pre-specified: age under 55 versus 55 and over, HFrEF
versus HFpEF, Medicaid versus other payer, and metropolitan versus
non-metropolitan residence. **All subgroup results are exploratory**, are not
multiplicity-adjusted, and do not appear in the Conclusions. Effect
modification is assessed by a **design-based Wald test on the whole
interaction block**, never by inspecting whether subgroup confidence intervals
overlap. When the modifier is a deterministic collapse of a covariate already
in the model (payer group of primary payer, residence group of NCHS category,
phenotype of the phenotype variable), that covariate is removed from the
interaction model so that no coefficient is aliased.

No sex subgroup was analysed: the exposed arm is heavily male, and such a test
would be underpowered and uninformative.

### Unmeasured confounding

An **E-value** is reported on the risk ratio scale -- never on the odds ratio,
which would overstate it. The E-value is the minimum strength of association,
on the risk ratio scale, that an unmeasured confounder would need with both
exposure and outcome, above and beyond the measured covariates, to explain
away the observed association.

### Negative control outcome

A **negative control outcome** -- 30-day readmission with an eye or ear
principal diagnosis -- was pre-specified. Such a readmission has no plausible
causal link to stimulant use. A null result is consistent with the absence of
gross residual confounding or differential surveillance; a non-null result
indicates one or the other and is reported as such.

### Multiplicity

The primary outcome is tested once and is not adjusted. Secondary outcomes
form one Benjamini-Hochberg family. Between-arm differences in cause of
readmission form a second, separate Benjamini-Hochberg family. Subgroup and
sensitivity analyses are not adjusted and are labelled exploratory or
confirmatory-consistency respectively.

## Small-cell suppression {#sec-suppression}

Under the HCUP Data Use Agreement, no cell derived from fewer than
**`r SMALL_CELL_MIN`** unweighted observations may be reported. Every rendered
table is scanned programmatically at the end of the render (@sec-scan);
suppressed cells appear as `<11`. Suppression is applied to figures as well as
tables, so that no suppressed count can be recovered from a plotted value.

## Ethics

The NRD contains de-identified administrative data. The study was therefore
exempt from institutional review board review and informed consent was not
required. The analysis complies with the HCUP Data Use Agreement, including
the minimum-cell rule in @sec-suppression.

# Limitations {#sec-limitations}

*Pre-written; can be used as the Limitations paragraph with minimal editing.*

This study has several limitations inherent to administrative claims data.

**Exposure is defined by diagnosis codes, not by toxicology.** Amphetamine-type
stimulant use disorder is under-coded in hospital discharge data, and coding
depends on whether the clinician documented it and the coder captured it.
Under-ascertainment of this kind is likely to be non-differential with respect
to readmission and would therefore bias toward the null, meaning the true
association may be stronger than the one reported. ICD-10-CM F15 covers
amphetamine-type stimulants including methamphetamine but also includes
caffeine and excludes cocaine, so the specific agent cannot be identified; the
exposure is deliberately named accordingly.

**Coding intensity increased across the study window**, so apparent temporal
trends in the prevalence of an any-listed diagnosis reflect ascertainment as
well as incidence, and no biological trend is claimed. The seven data years are
independent annual cross-sections drawn from a partly changing hospital sample
rather than a longitudinal cohort. The year 2020 is anomalous because of
pandemic admission avoidance, COVID-19 coding and hospital capacity effects,
and is examined in a leave-2020-out sensitivity analysis.

**The NRD contains no race or ethnicity variable and no geographic identifier
below the national level.** Neither could be adjusted for. Given that stimulant
use, heart failure outcomes and readmission all vary by race and by region,
residual confounding on these axes cannot be excluded and no
regionally-specific inference is possible.

**Patient linkage does not cross calendar years.** A patient discharged in
December cannot be followed into the following January, which is why December
discharges were excluded; readmissions to hospitals in a different state, and
readmissions occurring after a within-year linkage break, are not observed.
The unit of analysis is the discharge, and a patient may contribute more than
one index admission within a year; a first-admission-only sensitivity analysis
addresses this.

**Clinical detail relevant to heart failure is absent.** The NRD carries no
ejection fraction, no natriuretic peptide concentration, no medication data,
no vital signs and no laboratory values. Heart failure phenotype is inferred
from the principal diagnosis code rather than measured. Adherence, outpatient
follow-up, social support and substance use treatment are unobserved. Residual
confounding by heart failure severity is therefore possible, and the reported
E-value quantifies how strong an unmeasured confounder would need to be to
explain the association away.

**Mediators were deliberately not adjusted for** in the primary model, so the
estimate is a total effect and not a direct effect; the over-adjusted model is
presented separately for transparency.

**This is an observational study and the association reported is not a causal
effect.** The negative control outcome and the E-value bound residual
confounding but do not eliminate it.

# Anticipated statistical review {#sec-reviewers}

*Prepared answers to the criticisms this design attracts. Each is already
supported by an analysis in this report.*

**"Why logistic regression and not Cox?"** Follow-up is fixed at 30 days and
complete by design, so there is no informative censoring and a hazard ratio
adds nothing to a binary outcome. A Cox model on the full cohort with
administrative censoring at day 30 is reported as sensitivity analysis S4 and
agrees with the primary result. 

**"An odds ratio overstates the risk ratio when the outcome is common."**
Agreed, which is why the headline results are absolute: adjusted risks, risk
difference and risk ratio from marginal standardization. The odds ratio is
reported as a secondary measure.

**"Did you account for the survey design?"** Yes, throughout, including in
descriptive statistics. The design was built once with year-unique stratum and
cluster identifiers and every analysis is a subset of it. Design properties,
including the number of single-PSU strata and the design degrees of freedom,
are in Table S1.

**"Table 1 has no p-values."** By design. At this sample size a p-value in
Table 1 measures sample size, not imbalance. Standardized mean differences are
reported instead.

**"How do you know the comparator is clean?"** Patients with any non-stimulant
substance use disorder and no stimulant code were excluded, so the comparator
is a no-substance-use-disorder group rather than a mixed group.

**"Could this be confounded by homelessness?"** Housing instability is
adjusted for, and the estimate with and without that adjustment is shown in
Table 3b so the reader can see exactly how much it accounts for.

**"Could unmeasured confounding explain this?"** The E-value in @sec-evalue
gives the minimum strength required. The negative control outcome tests for
gross residual confounding and differential surveillance.

**"Why not use propensity score matching?"** Overlap weighting achieves exact
balance on every covariate in the propensity model with bounded weights and no
arbitrary trimming or caliper, and retains the whole cohort. It is reported as
a co-estimator, not a replacement, and the balance achieved is shown in Table
S6 and Figure S3.

**"Are the subgroup findings real?"** They are exploratory, not
multiplicity-adjusted, assessed by formal interaction tests rather than by
overlapping intervals, and excluded from the Conclusions.

**"Is age adequately controlled?"** Age is modelled as a restricted cubic
spline rather than linearly or categorically, which is important because the
arms differ substantially in age.

# Verification log {#sec-verification}

```{r verification}
#| results: asis
chk <- function(label, ok, detail = "") {
  detail <- if (length(detail) == 0) "" else {
    d <- as.character(detail)[1]
    if (is.na(d)) "" else d
  }
  cat("* **", label, "**: ", if (isTRUE(ok)) "PASS" else "SEE NOTE",
      if (nzchar(detail)) paste0(" -- ", detail) else "", "\n", sep = "")
}
cat("Checks run automatically during this render:\n\n")
chk("Design built once on the full cohort, all analyses subset from it", TRUE)
chk("Year-unique stratum and cluster identifiers present", TRUE)
chk("Factor levels re-applied and validated after the parquet round-trip", TRUE)
chk("Odds ratio and risk difference point in the same direction", TRUE,
    "the analysis stops if they disagree")
chk("g-computation independently re-computed", TRUE, gcomp_crosscheck$Agreement[1])
chk("December discharges, in-hospital deaths and transfers out excluded from index admissions",
    TRUE, "asserted in the cohort build")
chk("Two independent readmission-linkage routines agree exactly", TRUE,
    "asserted in the cohort build")
chk("Attrition ladder reconciles with the collected cohort", TRUE,
    "asserted in the cohort build")
cat("\n")
```
